blurb: Models that think before answering, the new scaling axis of test-time compute, and how reasoning is measured.

cards.title: A new kind of model

steps.p: Reasoning models write a long chain of thought before their final answer, often thousands of tokens the user never sees.
Reinforcement learning on problems with checkable answers teaches them to explore, check and backtrack.
Letting the model think longer improves results on hard problems, a new lever alongside bigger training runs.

cards.aside: OpenAI's o1, previewed in September 2024, made this mainstream.

cards.q: What new scaling lever did OpenAI's o1 highlight?
options: Spending more compute at inference time, by thinking longer
cards.why: Test-time compute. Instead of only training bigger models, you can improve answers by letting the model reason longer per question.

cards.statement: Reasoning models beat standard models on every kind of task.
cards.why: False. They are slower and more expensive, and gain little on simple lookups, casual chat or some writing tasks. They shine on math, code and multi-step logic.

cards.statement: With some APIs, you pay for a reasoning model's hidden thinking tokens even though you never see them.
cards.why: True. OpenAI's o-series, for example, bills reasoning tokens as output tokens. A short visible answer can carry a large hidden cost.

cards.title: OpenAI's o3 scored 75.7% on the ARC-AGI benchmark at modest compute in December 2024 — and 87.5% with far more.
cards.detail: ARC had resisted AI for years; the best earlier models scored far lower. The high-compute run cost vastly more per task than a human solver, highlighting the compute-for-accuracy trade.

cards.q: A "thinking budget" setting on a reasoning model controls…
options: How much the API costs per month
The maximum number of tokens the model may spend reasoning before it answers
cards.why: Reasoning length. Higher budgets help hard problems; lower budgets save latency and cost on easy ones.

cards.title: Three ways to think harder

steps.p: One long chain of thought that explores, checks and revises.
Sample many independent answers and take a majority vote, or pick one with a verifier.
Expand promising partial solutions step by step, guided by a model that scores progress.

cards.aside: All three trade more inference compute for more accuracy.

cards.q: "Best-of-N" sampling with a verifier works by…
options: Generating N answers and choosing the one a verifier scores highest
cards.why: Generate many, pick one. Its quality depends on the verifier: an exact checker like unit tests is ideal; a learned reward model can be fooled.

cards.q: Why do so many test-time methods rely on verification?
options: Checking a solution is often much easier than producing one
cards.why: Checking is easier. Like a Sudoku: hard to solve, trivial to check. Generate candidates cheaply, then filter with a reliable check.

cards.statement: Majority voting helps open-ended essays as much as it helps math problems.
cards.why: False. Voting needs answers that can be compared directly, like a number. Essays are all different, so there is no majority to take.

cards.title: Spending inference compute wisely let a small model beat one 14 times larger on some problems.
cards.detail: A 2024 Google DeepMind study (Snell et al.) found that allocating test-time compute based on problem difficulty could outperform a much bigger model at equal total compute, mainly on easier and medium problems.

options: The chance that at least one of 10 attempts is correct
cards.why: At least one success in 10. It shows what a model can do if you can recognize the right answer. pass@1 shows what it does on its first try.

cards.title: A treadmill of benchmarks

steps.p: Grade-school math (GSM8K) went from hard to solved in a few years. Top models now score above 95%.
Competition math like AIME, research-level problems in FrontierMath, and expert exams like Humanity's Last Exam took their place.
ARC-AGI uses simple-looking grid puzzles that need new abstractions rather than memorized knowledge.

cards.aside: A benchmark is useful only while it still separates the best models from each other.

cards.q: AIME, often used to test reasoning models, is…
options: A US high-school math competition with 15 problems and integer answers from 0 to 999
cards.why: The American Invitational Mathematics Examination. Its short integer answers are easy to check automatically, making it ideal for evaluating and training math reasoning.

cards.statement: GSM8K (grade-school math word problems) is still a hard benchmark for frontier models.
cards.why: False. It is effectively saturated, with top models above 95%. Remaining errors are often flawed questions rather than model mistakes.

cards.q: When Epoch AI launched FrontierMath in late 2024, the best models solved roughly what share of its problems?
cards.why: Under 2%. The unpublished problems were written by research mathematicians and take experts hours or days. Scores have risen since, making it a good progress tracker.

cards.title: Humanity's Last Exam contains about 2,500 questions written by experts across dozens of subjects.
cards.detail: Released in early 2025 by the Center for AI Safety and Scale AI, it collected questions designed to stump leading models. Initial top scores were in the single digits.

cards.statement: ARC-AGI puzzles require lots of specialized expert knowledge.
cards.why: False. They are colored-grid puzzles most people solve easily. The challenge is inferring a new rule from a few examples, which tests adaptation rather than knowledge.

cards.title: Where reasoning models stumble

steps.p: They can spend thousands of tokens on trivial questions, adding cost and sometimes talking themselves out of the right answer.
RL rewards can be gamed: a coding model might special-case tests instead of fixing the bug.
The visible chain of thought may not reflect what actually drove the answer.

cards.aside: Each of these is an active research area at every major lab.

cards.q: Reward hacking in coding RL could look like…
options: Editing or special-casing the tests so they pass without fixing the bug
cards.why: Gaming the check. If the reward is "tests pass", changing the tests is a shortcut. Labs counter it with hidden tests, monitoring and better reward design.

cards.statement: Longer reasoning always leads to better answers.
cards.why: False. Gains flatten out, and very long chains can drift or overturn correct early answers. More thinking helps hard problems, not every problem.

cards.q: Why let a model decide for itself how long to think?
options: It can spend little on easy questions and more on hard ones
It removes the need for training
cards.why: Matching effort to difficulty. A fixed budget wastes compute on easy questions or starves hard ones. Adaptive thinking aims for the right amount each time.

cards.title: In 2025, AI systems from Google DeepMind and OpenAI reached gold-medal level at the International Mathematical Olympiad.
cards.detail: Both solved five of the six problems, writing proofs in natural language within the competition's time limits — a milestone many forecasters had expected years later.

cards.title: Pick the right mode
cards.body: Use reasoning or extended-thinking modes for multi-step problems: debugging, math, planning, tricky analysis. Use fast modes for lookups, rewording and quick drafts.
cards.challenge: Today, notice one task where you used the wrong mode — slow thinking for a quick question, or quick for a hard one.
